wars.name: Civil wars of 193-197
wars.outcome: Septimius Severus defeats Didius Julianus (193), Pescennius Niger (194) and Clodius Albinus (197) and founds the Severan dynasty
wars.summary: The wars of succession after the murder of Pertinax, in which the Danubian army's candidate Septimius Severus defeated the Syrian army's Pescennius Niger and then the British army's Clodius Albinus.
wars.detail: Severus' strategy was masterly: he neutralised Albinus with the title of Caesar, seized Rome, and sent his generals against Niger while holding the Bosporus with a long siege of Byzantium. Victory at Issus (194) gave him the East. When Albinus, cut out of the succession, crossed into Gaul, Severus marched west and won at Lugdunum (197), the largest battle between Roman armies on record. The wars established the precedent that provincial armies made emperors, and Severus' purges and confiscations funded his rule. Sides: Severans versus Nigerians and Albinians (all Roman).

phases.t: Julianus overthrown; Severus takes Rome
War against Niger: Cyzicus, Nicaea, Issus
Siege of Byzantium
War against Albinus: Lugdunum

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Parthian wars of Septimius Severus
wars.outcome: Roman victory; sack of Ctesiphon; creation of the province of Mesopotamia; Hatra unconquered
wars.summary: Severus' two eastern wars: a punitive campaign of 195 against Osroene and Adiabene, and the invasion of 197-198 that sacked Ctesiphon, followed by two failed sieges of Hatra.
wars.detail: The wars added Mesopotamia (Nisibis, Singara) to the empire, which Dio criticised as a permanent cause of war. By humiliating the Arsacids they contributed to the conditions for the Sasanian takeover in 224.

phases.t: Campaign against Osroene and Adiabene
Invasion of Babylonia; sack of Ctesiphon
Sieges of Hatra

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Severus' Caledonian war
wars.outcome: Inconclusive; Caledonians and Maeatae submit and revolt; Caracalla withdraws to Hadrian's Wall after Severus' death
wars.summary: The imperial expedition of Severus, Caracalla and Geta against the Caledonii and Maeatae beyond the Antonine line, based at York, with a legionary base at Carpow on the Tay.
wars.detail: Dio reports heavy losses to guerrilla warfare in bogs and forests. The war probably aimed at conquest; it ended with Severus' death at York in 211 and Caracalla's peace, after which the northern frontier was quiet for most of the third century.

phases.t: Arrival and first campaign; submission of the Caledonians
Revolt and genocidal punitive campaign
Severus dies; Caracalla makes peace

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Parthian war of Caracalla and Macrinus
wars.outcome: Indecisive; Macrinus pays Artabanus IV 200 million sesterces
wars.summary: Caracalla's invasion of Media and Adiabene after his marriage proposal was refused, ended by his murder and by Macrinus' bloody draw at Nisibis.

phases.t: Caracalla's raid into Media; tombs at Arbela desecrated
Caracalla murdered; battle of Nisibis; peace

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: First Sasanian war (Ardashir and Severus Alexander)
wars.outcome: Stalemate; Mesopotamia preserved at heavy cost
wars.summary: The first war between Rome and the new Sasanian dynasty: Ardashir's invasion of Mesopotamia and Alexander's three-column counter-offensive of 232.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: German war of Severus Alexander and Maximinus
wars.outcome: Roman punitive victories, including the battle at the Harzhorn; Maximinus takes the title Germanicus Maximus
wars.summary: Campaigns on the Rhine against Germanic incursions of 233-234, begun by Severus Alexander (murdered at Mogontiacum) and carried deep into Germany by Maximinus, then continued on the Danube against Sarmatians and Dacians.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Civil war of 238 (Year of the Six Emperors)
wars.outcome: Maximinus killed at Aquileia; Pupienus and Balbinus murdered; Gordian III sole emperor
wars.summary: The Senate's rebellion against Maximinus Thrax, begun by the Gordians' revolt in Africa and ending with the Praetorians installing Gordian III.

phases.t: Gordians proclaimed at Thysdrus; defeated at Carthage
Pupienus and Balbinus; siege of Aquileia
Praetorians murder the senatorial emperors

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Persian war of Gordian III
wars.outcome: Persian victory at Misiche; Gordian III dies; Philip pays 500,000 aurei
wars.summary: After the Sasanians took Hatra, Nisibis and Carrhae, Gordian III's great expedition won at Rhesaina but was defeated at Misiche; Philip the Arab made peace.

wars.name: Gothic war of Decius
wars.outcome: Gothic victory; Decius killed at Abritus; Gallus pays tribute
wars.summary: The invasion of Moesia and Thrace by Cniva's Goths and their allies, culminating in the sack of Philippopolis and the death of Decius at Abritus.
wars.detail: Preceded by the first Gothic raid on Histria (238), the war was the first in which a Germanic people killed a Roman emperor.

wars.name: Shapur I's second and third wars against Rome
wars.outcome: Sasanian victories: Barbalissos, Antioch sacked, Dura destroyed, Valerian captured; Odaenathus' counter-offensives restore the Roman East
wars.summary: Shapur I's devastating invasions of Syria, Cappadocia and Cilicia, including the capture of Valerian at Edessa in 260, followed by Odaenathus of Palmyra's counterattacks to Ctesiphon.

phases.t: Second campaign: Barbalissos, sack of Antioch, Dura-Europos
Third campaign: Edessa and capture of Valerian; raids into Cilicia and Cappadocia
Odaenathus' counter-offensives

wars.name: Gothic and Herulian invasions
wars.outcome: After two decades of raids by land and sea, Roman victories at the Nestus, Naissus and beyond the Danube end the great invasions
wars.summary: Seaborne raids by Boranoi, Goths and Heruli across the Black Sea and Aegean (Pityus, Trapezus, Bithynia, Athens), and land invasions of the Balkans, ended by Gallienus, Claudius II and Aurelian.

phases.t: Black Sea raids: Pityus, Trapezus, Bithynia
Great Herulian raid; Athens sacked
Naissus and pursuit
Aurelian's victory beyond the Danube

wars.name: Alamannic and Juthungian invasions of Italy
wars.outcome: Invaders defeated at Milan (259), Lake Benacus (268), Fano and Pavia (271) after a defeat at Placentia
wars.summary: Repeated invasions of Italy by Alamanni and Juthungi through the Alpine passes, prompting the building of the Aurelian Walls.

wars.name: Wars against the Gallic Empire
wars.outcome: Aurelian defeats Tetricus at Châlons (274); Gaul, Britain and Spain reunited with the empire
wars.summary: The secession of the western provinces under Postumus, Victorinus and Tetricus, intermittent Roman attempts to recover them, and Aurelian's reconquest.
wars.detail: Gallienus' attempt c. 265 failed; Claudius II recovered Spain and Raetia's loyalty shifted. The Gallic regime never attacked Italy, focusing on Rhine defence. Probus' Rhine campaigns of 277-278 are included here for continuity.

phases.t: Postumus' secession; Gallienus' failed recovery
Laelianus, Marius, Victorinus; Autun sacked
Aurelian's reconquest at Châlons

wars.name: Palmyrene war
wars.outcome: Aurelian conquers Palmyra; Zenobia captured; Palmyra sacked after a second revolt
wars.summary: Zenobia's expansion into Egypt and Asia Minor and Aurelian's reconquest of the East in 272, with the second revolt and sack of Palmyra in 273.

phases.t: Palmyrene conquest of Egypt and Asia Minor
Aurelian's campaign: Tyana, Immae, Emesa, siege of Palmyra
Second revolt; sack of Palmyra; Firmus in Egypt

scholarship: Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

wars.name: Carausian revolt
wars.outcome: Constantius I recovers Britain after the defeat of Allectus
wars.summary: The ten-year secession of Britain and parts of northern Gaul under Carausius and Allectus, ended by Constantius' capture of Boulogne (293) and the invasion of 296.

wars.name: Persian war of Galerius and Narseh
wars.outcome: Decisive Roman victory; Peace of Nisibis gives Rome five Transtigritane regions and control of Armenia and Iberia
wars.summary: Narseh's invasion of Armenia and Mesopotamia, Galerius' defeat near Callinicum, and his crushing victory in Armenia in 298 followed by the Peace of Nisibis.

wars.name: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy
wars.outcome: Collapse of the tetrarchic system; Constantine controls the West and Licinius the East by 313
wars.summary: The struggles following the abdications of 305: the usurpations of Constantine and Maxentius (306), the failures of Severus and Galerius in Italy (307), the Carnuntum settlement (308), the fall of Maximian (310), Constantine's conquest of Italy (312) and Licinius' defeat of Maximinus Daia (313).

phases.t: Usurpations of Constantine and Maxentius; Severus and Galerius fail in Italy
Carnuntum settlement; Domitius Alexander; Maximian's end
Constantine invades Italy: Turin, Verona, Milvian Bridge
Licinius defeats Maximinus Daia

wars.name: Wars of Constantine and Licinius
wars.outcome: Constantine sole emperor after Chrysopolis (324); Licinius executed (325)
wars.summary: Two wars between the Augusti: the first (316-317) gave Constantine the Balkans after Cibalae and Mardia; the second (324), presented by Eusebius as a holy war, ended with Adrianople, the Hellespont and Chrysopolis.

phases.t: First war: Cibalae, Mardia; peace of Serdica
Second war: Adrianople, Hellespont, Chrysopolis

wars.name: Constantine's Gothic and Sarmatian war
wars.outcome: Roman victory; treaty of 332 with the Tervingi; settlement of Sarmatian refugees
wars.summary: Constantine's reassertion of Roman power north of the lower Danube: the bridge at Oescus (328), Constantine II's victory over the Tervingi (332), the ensuing treaty and the reception of 300,000 Sarmatians (334).

wars.name: Persian war of Constantius II and Shapur II
wars.outcome: Stalemate for two decades; Shapur takes Amida, Singara and Bezabde (359-360)
wars.summary: A long war of sieges and raids in northern Mesopotamia: Shapur's three sieges of Nisibis (338, 346, 350), the night battle of Singara (344 or 348), and his offensive of 359-360 that took Amida, Singara and Bezabde.
wars.detail: Constantius' strategy was defensive, relying on fortified cities. The war was interrupted by Shapur's eastern wars and by Roman civil war (350-353), and was renewed by Julian in 363 (see julian_persian_war).

phases.t: Sieges of Nisibis; Singara
Truce in practice; Shapur fights in the east, Constantius in the west
Shapur's offensive: Amida, Singara, Bezabde

scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

wars.name: Civil war against Magnentius
wars.outcome: Constantius II defeats Magnentius at Mursa and Mons Seleucus; sole emperor
wars.summary: The usurpation of Magnentius in the West after the murder of Constans, the brief reigns of Vetranio and Nepotianus, and Constantius' victory at Mursa (351), one of the bloodiest battles of Roman history.

wars.name: Julian's Alamannic and Frankish wars
wars.outcome: Rhine frontier restored; Chnodomar captured at Strasbourg; Frankish Salii settled in Toxandria
wars.summary: Julian's campaigns as Caesar in Gaul: relief of Cologne and Autun, the victory of Strasbourg (357), crossings of the Rhine, and treaties with Alamannic and Frankish kings.

wars.name: Julian's Persian expedition
wars.outcome: Julian killed; Jovian cedes Nisibis, Singara and the Transtigritane regions
wars.summary: Julian's invasion of Persia with perhaps 65,000 men down the Euphrates to Ctesiphon, his death during the retreat, and Jovian's humiliating peace.

wars.name: Revolt of Procopius
wars.outcome: Procopius defeated at Thyatira and Nacolia and executed
wars.summary: The usurpation of Julian's relative Procopius at Constantinople, supported by Gothic troops, against Valens.

wars.name: Valens' Gothic war
wars.outcome: Treaty on the Danube between Valens and Athanaric; subsidies ended and trade restricted
wars.summary: Valens' punitive campaigns north of the Danube against the Tervingi who had supported Procopius.

wars.name: Revolt of Firmus
wars.outcome: Count Theodosius suppresses the revolt; Firmus commits suicide
wars.summary: The rebellion of the Moorish prince Firmus in Mauretania, provoked by the abuses of the comes Africae Romanus.

wars.name: Quadic and Sarmatian war
wars.outcome: Roman punitive campaign; Valentinian I dies at Brigetio
wars.summary: Invasion of Pannonia by the Quadi and Sarmatians after the murder of the Quadic king Gabinius, answered by Valentinian's campaign of 375.

wars.name: Gothic war of 376-382
wars.outcome: Roman catastrophe at Adrianople; treaty of 382 settles the Goths within the empire as an autonomous people
wars.summary: The war that began when Tervingian refugees from the Huns, abused by Roman officials, revolted in Thrace; it brought the death of Valens and most of the eastern field army at Adrianople and ended with Theodosius' treaty of 382.
wars.detail: Ammianus' narrative ends with Adrianople; for 379-382 we depend on Zosimus, Themistius and church historians. Theodosius rebuilt the army but could not defeat the Goths decisively, and the settlement of 382 created a Gothic population within the empire that produced Alaric's revolt in 395.

phases.t: Crossing of the Danube; Marcianople; Ad Salices
Argentaria; Adrianople; Goths fail before Constantinople
Theodosius' war of containment; treaty of 3 October 382

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

wars.name: Civil war against Magnus Maximus
wars.outcome: Theodosius defeats Maximus at Siscia and Poetovio; Maximus executed at Aquileia
wars.summary: Magnus Maximus' usurpation in Britain and Gaul (383), uneasy recognition (384-387), invasion of Italy (387) and defeat by Theodosius (388).

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

wars.name: Civil war against Eugenius
wars.outcome: Theodosius wins at the Frigidus; Eugenius executed and Arbogast commits suicide
wars.summary: Following the death of Valentinian II, Arbogast's emperor Eugenius held the West for two years with pagan senatorial support until Theodosius' victory at the Frigidus.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)

campaigns.name: Severus' advance against Pescennius Niger
campaigns.strength: Danubian legions and vexillations; strength unknown
campaigns.summary: From Rome Severus marched overland through Illyricum and Thrace to Perinthus, while his generals crossed into Asia, won at Cyzicus and Nicaea, forced the Taurus passes and destroyed Niger at Issus.

path.note: Severus leaves Rome about a month after arriving

path.t: Antioch: Niger caught and killed nearby

campaigns.note: Severus himself remained mostly in Thrace; the Asian campaign was conducted by Anullinus and Candidus. Route through Illyricum inferred.

campaigns.name: Severus' march against Clodius Albinus
campaigns.strength: Danubian and Rhine legions; Dio's 150,000 is exaggerated
campaigns.summary: After making Caracalla Caesar at Viminacium, Severus marched west through Pannonia, Noricum and Raetia into Gaul and met Albinus north of Lugdunum.
campaigns.note: Route through Noricum and Raetia follows indications in the HA and the logic of the road network; exact itinerary unknown.

campaigns.name: Severus' Mesopotamian campaign
campaigns.strength: Probably three Parthian legions plus vexillations, Osroene archers and a Euphrates river fleet
campaigns.summary: Severus sailed from Brundisium to Syria, relieved Nisibis, then descended the Euphrates in a fleet of boats to take Seleucia, Babylon and Ctesiphon, returning up the Tigris and failing before Hatra.

path.t: Nisibis: winter quarters and organisation of Mesopotamia

campaigns.note: Dio and Herodian differ on details; Herodian has the fleet drift to Ctesiphon by chance.

campaigns.name: Severus' Caledonian campaigns
campaigns.strength: Perhaps 40,000-50,000 including the British legions, Praetorians and vexillations; Dio claims 50,000 casualties
campaigns.summary: From York, Severus and Caracalla advanced through the eastern lowlands, crossed the Forth on a bridge of boats to the new base at Carpow and penetrated Strathmore toward the north-east, building a line of large marching camps.

path.t: Cramond: supply base on the Forth
Carpow: legionary base on the Tay
path.note: Forth crossed by a pontoon bridge
Dio: Severus approached the extremity of the island

campaigns.note: Northern limit uncertain; the line of 'Severan' 63-acre and 130-acre camps is dated by association, not inscriptions.

campaigns.name: Gordian III's Persian expedition
campaigns.strength: Large army with Germanic and Gothic contingents (ŠKZ); numbers unknown
campaigns.summary: Gordian marched from Rome through the Balkans to Antioch, recovered Carrhae and Nisibis after Rhesaina, then advanced down the Euphrates toward Ctesiphon and was defeated at Misiche.

campaigns.name: Decius against Cniva
campaigns.summary: Decius relieved Nicopolis ad Istrum, pursued Cniva over the Haemus, was surprised near Beroe, regrouped and in 251 caught the returning Goths near Abritus, where he was killed.
campaigns.note: Sequence reconstructed from Jordanes, Zosimus and the Dexippus fragments; details uncertain.

campaigns.name: Shapur I's third campaign
campaigns.summary: Shapur advanced from Ctesiphon through Mesopotamia, besieged Edessa and Carrhae, captured Valerian, then raided Syria, Cilicia and Cappadocia before being harried by Odaenathus on his return across the Euphrates.
campaigns.note: The ŠKZ lists captured cities rather than a route; sequence reconstructed.

campaigns.name: Aurelian's campaign against Zenobia
campaigns.strength: Field army including Dalmatian and Moorish cavalry, Moesian and Pannonian legions, Palestinian clubmen
campaigns.summary: Aurelian crossed into Asia, took Tyana, forced the Cilician Gates, defeated Zabdas' cataphracts at Immae and Emesa, and besieged Palmyra until Zenobia's capture.

campaigns.name: Aurelian's campaign against Tetricus
campaigns.summary: Aurelian marched from Italy over the Alps into Gaul and destroyed the Gallic army at the Catalaunian Fields.

campaigns.name: Galerius' Persian campaign
campaigns.summary: With a new army raised in Illyricum, Galerius advanced through Cappadocia into Armenia, routed Narseh and captured his family, then pushed through Media and Adiabene and returned via Mesopotamia.
campaigns.note: Route beyond Armenia, and whether Galerius reached Ctesiphon, are uncertain.

campaigns.name: Constantine's invasion of Italy
campaigns.strength: c. 40,000 (modern estimate); a quarter of his army according to the panegyric of 313
campaigns.summary: Constantine crossed the Alps from Gaul, stormed Segusio, won at Turin and Verona, then marched down the Via Aemilia and Via Flaminia to defeat Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge.

path.t: Via Flaminia through the Apennines (Furlo pass)

campaigns.note: Alpine pass (Mont Genèvre or Mont Cenis) uncertain.

campaigns.name: Licinius against Maximinus Daia
campaigns.summary: From the Milan conference Licinius hurried east, defeated Maximinus at Tzirallum in Thrace, published the Milan letter at Nicomedia and pursued his rival to Tarsus.

campaigns.name: Constantine's war against Licinius
campaigns.strength: 120,000 foot and 10,000 horse (Zosimus, inflated); fleet of 200 ships under Crispus
campaigns.summary: From Thessalonica Constantine forced the Hebrus at Adrianople, besieged Byzantium while Crispus won the Hellespont, then crossed the Bosporus to win at Chrysopolis.

campaigns.name: Constantius II against Magnentius
campaigns.summary: Leaving the Persian front, Constantius marched west through Asia Minor and Thrace, accepted Vetranio's abdication at Naissus, and met Magnentius on the Drava at Mursa.

campaigns.name: Julian's campaign of 357
campaigns.summary: From winter quarters at Sens, Julian moved to the Rhine, rebuilt Tres Tabernae, defeated Chnodomar at Strasbourg, crossed the Rhine near Mainz and ended the year besieging Frankish raiders on the Meuse before wintering at Paris.

path.t: Across the Rhine: raid into Alamannic lands
Meuse forts: Frankish raiders besieged for 54 days

campaigns.note: Location of the Meuse forts unknown.

campaigns.name: Julian's Persian expedition
campaigns.strength: c. 65,000 (Zosimus) including Procopius' northern force of 18,000-30,000; river fleet of over 1,000 ships
campaigns.summary: Julian marched from Antioch to Carrhae, sent Procopius north, descended the Euphrates with his fleet, crossed to the Tigris by canal, won before Ctesiphon, burned his fleet, and died during the retreat; Jovian led the army home via Hatra and Nisibis.

path.t: Dura on the Tigris: Jovian's treaty

campaigns.note: Points between Ctesiphon and the retreat are approximate.

campaigns.name: Gothic movements, 376-378
campaigns.strength: Tervingi perhaps 15,000-20,000 warriors with families; joined by Greuthungi, Alans and some Huns
campaigns.summary: The Tervingi crossed the Danube, broke out after Lupicinus' treachery at Marcianople, ranged through Thrace, fought at Ad Salices, and destroyed Valens' army near Adrianople before failing at Constantinople.
campaigns.note: Order of Thracian movements in 377 is uncertain; Ad Salices location disputed.

campaigns.name: Theodosius' campaign against Magnus Maximus
campaigns.strength: Eastern army with large Gothic, Hunnic and Alan contingents
campaigns.summary: From Thessalonica Theodosius marched north-west up the Axius and Morava, crossed the Save at Siscia, beat Maximus' brother at Poetovio and took Maximus at Aquileia.

campaigns.name: Theodosius' campaign against Eugenius
campaigns.strength: Eastern army with c. 20,000 Gothic federates
campaigns.summary: Theodosius marched from Constantinople up the Balkan military road, forced the Julian Alps at Ad Pirum and won the two-day battle of the Frigidus.

polities.name: Juthungi
polities.summary: Germanic people north of the upper Danube in Raetia, probably a Suebic/Semnonian offshoot later counted among the Alamanni; invaded Italy in 260 and 270-271 and Raetia in the fourth and fifth centuries.

polities.name: Vandals
polities.summary: East Germanic people (Hasdingi and Silingi) in the middle Danube and Silesia region before their migration west in 406; fought Aurelian and Probus and were settled in Pannonia by Constantine according to Jordanes. Continued as vandal_kingdom from 429.

polities.name: Chionites
polities.summary: Central Asian nomads (Xyon) on Persia's north-eastern frontier, fought and then allied by Shapur II; their king Grumbates fought at Amida in 359. Possibly related to the later Kidarites and Hephthalites.

polities.name: Isaurians
polities.summary: Mountain people of the Taurus in southern Anatolia, notorious for banditry and revolts against Roman authority from the third to the sixth centuries, yet also an important recruiting ground (the emperor Zeno was Isaurian).

polities.name: Bagaudae
polities.summary: Rural insurgents and self-help bands in Gaul and later Spain, suppressed by Maximian in 285-286 and reappearing in the fifth century; their nature (peasant revolt, banditry, local defence) is debated.
